'''Sharon Matola''' (June 3, 1954 – March 21, 2021)<ref>{{cite web |last1=Staff |first1=B. B. N. |title=Belize mourns immeasurable loss as world renowned conservationist and Belize Zoo Founder, Sharon Matola, passes away |url=https://www.breakingbelizenews.com/2021/03/21/belize-mourns-immeasurable-loss-as-world-renowned-conservationist-and-belize-zoo-founder-sharon-matola-passes-away1/ |website=Belize News and Opinion on www.breakingbelizenews.com |access-date=March 22, 2021 |date=March 21, 2021 |archive-date=March 21, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321212635/https://www.breakingbelizenews.com/2021/03/21/belize-mourns-immeasurable-loss-as-world-renowned-conservationist-and-belize-zoo-founder-sharon-matola-passes-away1/ |url-status=live }}</ref> was an American-born Belizean [[biologist]], [[environmentalist]], and [[zookeeper]]. She was the founding director of the [[Belize Zoo|Belize Zoo and Tropical Education Center]], a zoo which was started in 1983 to protect native animals that had been used in a documentary film in [[Belize]].<ref name=":0">http://www.bfbs-radio.com/pages/extranet/sharon-matola-i-1303.php, BFBS radio presenters, Sharon Matola, Retrieved September 6, 2010. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101026231221/http://bfbs-radio.com/pages/extranet/sharon-matola-i-1303.php |date=October 26, 2010 }}</ref> Matola graduated from [[New College of Florida]] in 1981 with a degree in [[biology]].

==Early life==
Matola was born in [[Baltimore]], [[Maryland]], on June 3, 1954.<ref name=langer20210331>{{Cite news|last=Langer|first=Emily|title=Sharon Matola, devoted zookeeper and conservationist, dies at 66|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/sharon-matola-dead/2021/03/31/a09c8422-90e9-11eb-a74e-1f4cf89fd948_story.html|date=March 31, 2021|access-date=May 25, 2021|issn=0190-8286|archive-date=April 12, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412081438/https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/sharon-matola-dead/2021/03/31/a09c8422-90e9-11eb-a74e-1f4cf89fd948_story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Her father was a sales manager for the [[National Brewing Company]] and her mother was an administrative assistant.<ref name=langer20210331/> She showed great interest in animals and concern for their welfare from an early age.<ref name=langer20210331/>

After graduating from high school, Matola enlisted in the [[United States Air Force]], in which she received [[jungle]] [[survival training]].<ref name=langer20210331/> She then studied [[Russian language|Russian]] at the [[University of Iowa]] before transferring to the [[New College of Florida]] 
in [[Sarasota, Florida|Sarasota]], [[Florida]], from which she received a bachelor's degree in biology in 1981;<ref name=langer20210331/> while at the college, she studied fish [[taxonomy]] during a trip to Belize.<ref name=langer20210331/> After college, she became an assistant [[Lion taming|lion tamer]] at the [[Circus Hall of Fame]] before attending [[graduate school]] to study [[mycology]].<ref name=langer20210331/> She left graduate school for a job as an [[exotic dancer]] in a [[traveling circus]] in [[Mexico]], hoping to do biological field work during the day before dancing at night.<ref name=langer20210331/>

==Belize Zoo==
[[File:Portrait of Sharon Matola, 1988.jpg|thumb|Matola in 1988]]
[[File:Sharon Matola with her beloved Junior Buddy at The Belize Zoo, 2011-07-20.jpg|thumb|Matola hosted unforgettable encounters with Junior Buddy that transformed people's attitudes about [[jaguar]]s. Above, Matola and Junior Buddy on {{nowrap|July 20, 2011.}}]]
[[File:Sharon Matola with children at Junior Buddy's 5th Birthday Celebration at The Belize Zoo, 2012-02-21.jpg|thumb|Matola with children at Junior Buddy's fifth birthday celebration at the Belize Zoo in 2012.]]
Matola's job in Mexico brought her to the attention of filmmaker Richard Foster, who hired her in 1982 to care for 20 animals being used in the making of a wildlife documentary film. When shooting of the film was completed, she was left to decide how to dispose of the animals, by then habituated to humans and unsuited to release into the wild. On a whim, she decided to care for the animals by starting the [[Belize Zoo]], hung signs out on the road, asked a nearby restaurant to coax patrons into visiting the zoo,<ref name=langer20210331/> and waited to see who would show up. She soon realized that what Belizeans knew about Belizean wildlife at the time was often more myth than fact and that they were unaware that damage to the Belizean [[rainforest]] threatened the populations of Belizean animals.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Matola |first1=Sharon |title=Twenty Questions. The July Interview with Sharon Matola, Director of the Belize Zoo. |url=https://www.belizemagazine.com/edition11/english/e11_04questions.htm |website=BELIZEmagazine.com |publisher=Jomamas Outside Worldwide, Inc |access-date=March 27, 2021 |archive-date=April 19, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419164639/https://www.belizemagazine.com/edition11/english/e11_04questions.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> With the blessing of the [[Government of Belize]], which could not offer financial support, she began raising money from [[environmental groups]] to build and support the zoo.<ref>Discovery Channel. Ed. Huw Hennessy: "Insight Guide Belize." Insight Print Services (Pte) Ltd., 2000.</ref>

By 1996 the zoo was home to over 125 native species.<ref name=maynard>Maynard, Caitlin and Thane: "Rainforests and Reefs: A Kid's Eye View of the Tropics." Zoological Society of Cincinnati, Inc., 1996.</ref> Singer-songwriter [[Jimmy Buffett]] and actor [[Harrison Ford]] became supporters of the zoo.<ref name=langer20210331/> Before the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] struck in 2020, the zoo drew 75,000 visitors a year, half of them Belizeans,<ref name=langer20210331/> and in March 2021 the zoo housed 190 animals representing 45 species native to Belize, including the [[tapir]], [[jaguar]], [[spider monkey]], [[White-nosed coati|coati]], [[scarlet macaw]], [[jabiru stork]], and two species of [[crocodile]].<ref name=langer20210331/> The zoo's staff numbered 58 people before the pandemic struck, but dropped to 32 by March 2021 as the pandemic raged.<ref name=langer20210331/>

Thanks to her work at the zoo, Matola became known as the "[[Jane Goodall]] of jaguars"<ref name=langer20210331/> and the "Jane Goodall of Belize."<ref>{{Cite news|last=Kofman|first=Jeffrey|title=The 'Jane Goodall of Belize'|language=en-US|work=ABC News|url=https://abcnews.go.com/WN/story?id=3583187&page=1|date=June 9, 2008|access-date=May 25, 2021|archive-date=May 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210525155809/https://abcnews.go.com/WN/story?id=3583187&page=1|url-status=live}}</ref> The zoo eventually was renamed the Belize Zoo and Tropical Education Center,<ref name=langer20210331/> reflecting its mission of teaching people about Belize's wildlife.<ref name=maynard/>

== Other work ==
[[File:2009-12-31 BFBS-BFR Matola Music Show BATSUB Belize.jpg|thumb|Matola hosts her radio show at Airport Camp, {{nowrap|ca. 2009.}}]]
Matola served as a consultant for the filming of the 1986 movie ''[[The Mosquito Coast (film)|The Mosquito Coast]]'', bringing her and the Belize Zoo to the attention of Harrison Ford and prompting him to become a supporter.<ref name=langer20210331/>

Matola fought unsuccessfully to stop Belize's [[Chalillo Dam]] project;<ref name=langer20210331/> the dam was constructed between 2002 and 2005. Her struggle was documented in the 2008 book ''The Last Flight of the Scarlet Macaw: One Woman's Fight to Save the World's Most Beautiful Bird'' by [[Bruce Barcott]].<ref name=langer20210331/>

Matola began to contribute to [[BFBS]] Radio in Belize in 1992, starting with a popular wildlife series called ''Walk on the Wildside'', in which she explored the lives of Belize's flora and fauna.  She also had a weekly [[rock and roll]] radio show that she broadcast from Airport Camp — the home base for [[British Army Training and Support Unit Belize]] (BATSUB), in [[Ladyville, Belize|Ladyville]], Belize — until August 2011, when the government of the [[United Kingdom]] closed the camp.<ref name=":0" />

Matola wrote children's books centering around the character Hoodwink the [[Owl]].<ref name=langer20210331/>

==Personal life==

Matola's marriage to Jack Schreier ended in divorce.<ref name=langer20210331/> She had no children.<ref name=langer20210331/> She became a naturalized Belizean citizen, and lived on the zoo's property.<ref name=langer20210331/> She said that her favorite animal was the [[harpy eagle]].<ref name=langer20210331/>

== Death ==

Matola died of a [[heart attack]] at a hospital in [[Belmopan]], Belize, on March 21, 2021, at the age of 66.<ref name=langer20210331/>

== In media ==

"The Reef...and the Rainforest," a 1992 episode of the [[PBS]] television series ''[[Return to the Sea (TV series)|Return to the Sea]]'', includes an interview with Matola and footage of the Belize Zoo.
